pages.p:
When JavaScript meets an error, the program normally stops. With **try / catch** you can handle the problem and keep going.

Put risky code in the «try» block. If something goes wrong there, JavaScript jumps straight to the «catch» block. Code after the problem, inside «try», is skipped.
pages.tip: «JSON.parse» from unit 8 throws an error when the text is not valid JSON.

pages.p:
You can also make an error yourself with «throw new Error("text")». It stops the current function at once and jumps to the nearest «catch», even if that «catch» is outside of several functions.

The «catch» gets the error object. Its «message» property holds your text.
pages.tip: Use «throw» when a function gets a value it cannot work with.

pages.p:
A «finally» block runs at the end **whether or not** there was an error. It is good for things that must always happen, like a final message.

It even runs when the «try» block has a «return» inside.
pages.tip: If «try» has «return», the «finally» code still runs first, and then the function returns.

pages.p: A function can use try / catch inside, and «return» a safe value when something fails. The people who call it never see a crash.
pages.tip: Do not hide every error. Catch only where you know a good way to recover.

pages.h: Error names and your own errors
pages.p:
Every error has a «name» and a «message». JavaScript's own problems have names like «SyntaxError». Errors from «new Error» have the name «Error».

Using unit 10, you can even make your own kind of error with a class that extends «Error». Then «instanceof» tells you which kind it is.
pages.o:
SyntaxError
true
age must be 0 or more
pages.tip: Messages of JavaScript's own errors can differ between browsers, so do not rely on their exact text.

pages.p:
Some things take time, like loading data. JavaScript does not stop and wait. It keeps running the rest of the code, and comes back later.

«setTimeout(function, ms)» runs a function after some milliseconds (1000 ms is 1 second). This kind of code is called **asynchronous**.
pages.o:
1: start
2: end of the code
3: later
pages.tip: The code after «setTimeout» does not wait. It runs first.

pages.h: Promise: a value in the future
pages.p:
A **promise** is an object that stands for a result that is not ready yet. It starts **pending**. Later it is **fulfilled** with a value (you call «resolve»), or **rejected** with an error (you call «reject»).

Use «.then(...)» to say what to do when the value arrives.
pages.tip: Think of a promise as a ticket you get while your pizza is baking.

pages.p: When a promise is rejected, the function in «.then» is skipped. Use «.catch(...)» to handle the error. It gets the error object, just like in try / catch.
pages.tip: A promise can only finish once: either resolved or rejected.

pages.p:
«.then» gives back a new promise. So you can chain steps. What one step returns goes to the next step.

If a step throws an error, JavaScript skips the next «.then» steps and goes to the next «.catch». And if the «.catch» returns a value, the chain continues normally.
pages.tip: «Promise.resolve(x)» makes a promise that is already fulfilled with x.

pages.p:
Chains of «.then» get long. **async / await** is a cleaner way. Put «async» before a function. Inside it, «await» pauses **that function** until a promise is ready, and gives you the value.

The rest of the program keeps running while it waits.
pages.tip: You can only use «await» inside an «async» function.

pages.p: A rejected promise becomes a normal error at the «await». So you can use plain try / catch, the same as for any other error.
pages.tip: This reads like normal code from top to bottom. That is why people like it.

pages.p:
«Promise.all» takes an array of promises. They all run at the same time. You get a new promise that gives an array of all results, **in the same order**, once every one is done.

If one of them is rejected, «Promise.all» is rejected too.
pages.tip: It takes about 60 ms in total, not 120 ms, because the waits overlap.

pages.p: An «async» function always returns a promise. A normal «return 5» becomes a promise fulfilled with 5. The proof: the result has a «.then» method, so its type check says «function». The caller uses «await» or «.then» to get the value.
pages.tip: This is why a plain «console.log(five())» does not show 5.

hand.why: «throw» jumps out of «try» at once. The line that prints 2 is skipped, and «catch» prints 3.

hand.ans: Only when something in the «try» block throws an error
wrong: Only when the «try» block has a «return»
hand.why: «catch» is the plan B. It is skipped when «try» finishes without an error. For code that must always run, use «finally».

hand.q: Complete the line that makes an error.
hand.why: «new Error("text")» builds an error object. «throw» then sends it to the nearest «catch».
«check(5)» is fine. «check(50)» throws, so «catch» prints the message of the error.
First define the function, then call it inside «try», then handle the error in «catch».
«setTimeout» does not stop the program. A and C print now, and the timer function runs a little later.
The block that handles the problem is written «catch (error) { ... }».

hand.q: A promise was rejected. Which method handles that?
hand.why: «.catch» receives the error of a rejected promise. A «.then» function is for success only, and «.finish» does not exist.
The «.then» function never runs at once. The rest of the normal code finishes first, so «sync» comes before 6.

hand.q: Pause until the promise is ready.
hand.why: «await» waits for the promise and gives you its value. Without it, «v» would be the promise itself.
«f» runs until its «await», then pauses. The main code continues and prints out. Later «f» continues.

hand.q: What does an «async» function always return?
wrong: An array of all the awaited values
hand.why: Even if you write «return 5», the caller gets a promise that is fulfilled with 5. Use «await» or «.then» to read it.
A rejected promise throws at the «await». The line that prints fine is skipped and «catch» runs.

hand.code:
function wait(ms, v) { return new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms)); }
Promise.all([wait(30, "x"), wait(10, "y")]).then(r => console.log(r.join("")));
hand.why: «Promise.all» keeps the order of the array, not the order in which the promises finish.

hard.why: The «finally» block runs before the function really returns. So «finally» is printed first, then the returned value.
The throw inside «a» stops «a» and «b» at once. The error travels up to the nearest «catch».
"5", "7" and "[1,2]" are valid JSON. "oops" and "{bad" are not. The loop keeps going after each error.
Normal code runs first. Then the timers fire in order of their delay: 10 ms before 30 ms, not in the order they were written.
A «.catch» that returns a value fixes the chain. The next «.then» gets that value as normal.
Each «await» waits for its task to finish before the next line runs. So the tasks run one after the other.
Both tasks start together. B needs only 10 ms, so it prints first. «Promise.all» finishes after the slowest one, so end comes last.

hard.q: Why does this code not work?
hard.ans: «await» is used in a function that is not «async»
hard.why: «await» is only allowed inside an «async» function. Put «async» before «function load».
If any promise in «Promise.all» is rejected, the whole result is rejected. So the «.then» is skipped and «.catch» runs.
A class that extends Error makes errors of its own kind. «instanceof» recognises it, and «message» passes through.

items.symptom: It prints "Error: undefined" instead of the real message.
items.why: Throwing a plain text gives «catch» a string, which has no «message». Throw an error object: «new Error("...")».

items.symptom: It crashes with: ReferenceError: err is not defined.
items.why: The error variable is named «error» in the «catch» line. «err» is a different name that does not exist.

items.symptom: "later" appears at once, between start and end, instead of after 50 ms.
items.why: «console.log("later")» is called straight away. You must give «setTimeout» a function that it can call later, like an arrow function.

items.symptom: It prints "Got [object Promise]" instead of "Got hi".
items.why: Without «await», «v» is the promise itself, not the value inside it.

items.symptom: It prints undefined, but it should print 8.
items.why: An arrow function with curly braces needs «return». Otherwise the next step receives undefined.

items.symptom: It will not even start: SyntaxError about «await».
items.why: «await» only works inside an «async» function. The function needs the word «async» in front.

project.title: Age Checker
project.brief:
Write a function «checkAges(texts)». «texts» is an array of strings. Each string should contain a JSON number, like «"25"».

An item is **good** when it parses to a number from 0 to 120. It is **bad** when the text is not valid JSON, when the value is not a number (like «"null"», «"[1]"» or «"\"7\""», a text), or when the number is below 0 or above 120.

Return an array with two things: an array of the good ages (in the same order), and the count of bad items.

Example: «checkAges(["12", "oops", "30"])» is [[12, 30], 1].

The starter shows the plan: parse inside «try», «throw new Error» for a wrong number, and count the bad ones in «catch».

tests.label: text value and null are bad
